title: Through Participatory Clinical Clerkships at Warwick Medical School, UK
paragraphs: For thirteen weeks, from March 5 to May 31, I was given the opportunity to do clinical clerkships at University Hospitals Coventry (UHC), the teaching hospital of Warwick Medical School in Coventry, in central England. I had done an internship in diagnostic pathology in New England in the United States last summer, so my original motivation this time was to do a clerkship in the real England and broaden my perspective on healthcare around the world even further.

For the first four weeks I worked in the ER setting at Accident & Emergency (A&E). The A&E outpatient department of UHC consists of four sections: minor (10 consulting rooms) for mild cases, major (25 consulting rooms) for severe cases, resuscitation (6 beds) and paediatric (6 consulting rooms), and even in broad daylight these rooms were almost always full of people of all ages because of the walk-in patients flooding in. There, from morning to night I trained, with feedback from senior doctors on each case I saw first, in the whole process of narrowing down possible emergency diseases with the medical interview and physical examination as my main weapons and then working out an effective testing plan to differentiate them. With the large number and wide range of cases, the clerkship was quite eventful. For example, in one chest pain case I blushed at having failed to suspect pulmonary embolism, while in another case I regained confidence when another senior doctor told me with a smile that, as a result of the serial troponin T measurement I had listed in my plan, a rise had just been seen and a diagnosis of non-ST elevation MI had been made. Besides such practicality, the senior doctors often threw questions at me to confirm the pathophysiology related to the cases, and I think I was able to learn, through each of my assigned cases, what fundamental understanding that can be applied flexibly in clinical practice looks like.

For the next two weeks I rotated through Haematology, and first joined as a member of the team in the care of three of the patients being treated on the ward for haematological malignancies. One of the roles I was given was to grasp the long treatment history written in the chart and the many clinical parameters that change from moment to moment, combine that prior information with what I obtained from actual conversation and physical examination with each patient, extract the current problem list, and present it, with a case summary, at the case conference. Thanks to conversations about findings with the nurses on the same team and the checks and advice from the resident on my summary, I was in the end able to bring it to a standard worthy of the conference, and I savoured a small sense of accomplishment at having contributed somewhat to setting the direction of the patient's next steps of care. I also attended a lecture for residents in which everyone discussed peripheral blood smears together with the blood count data, which helped me review the basics of haematological morphology and the differential diagnosis of anaemia. I was also allowed to attend specialist outpatient clinics for particular blood diseases such as haemoglobinopathy, coagulation disease and DVT (deep venous thrombosis). What was very impressive was that the specialisation of nurses is established to a surprising degree, and that in some respects nurses even lead doctors, as in how the DVT nurse took the initiative in dealing with patients across departments, in a large part of the DVT diagnosis without relying on a doctor's judgment.

The remaining final six weeks I trained in the Pathology department. The training here was very flexible, and when I told the senior doctors that I was particularly interested in respiratory tumour pathology and bone marrow pathology, each pathologist gave me a research theme that could be completed in a month, so from the second week on I devoted my energy mainly to pursuing these two themes. I also attended autopsies, which are performed at a pace of at least three bodies a day, and took part in Mechanisms of Disease, a case-based PBL-style class that the pathology staff teach every week to first-year undergraduates. What surprised me in undergraduate education is that Warwick Medical School has no dissection curriculum, students interested in anatomy are told to attend autopsies on their own initiative, and the study of anatomy, histology, embryology and pathology is all covered in Mechanisms of Disease in the first year. I could not deny the impression that morphology has been pushed quite far into a corner of the curriculum, but I also thought that it might be an unavoidable sacrifice in order to put weight on developing sufficient clinical competence within the time constraint of four years.

The thoroughly patient-oriented clinical clerkships at this medical school not only contributed to improving my own clinical skills but also gave me a rare opportunity to recognise, in accordance with the actual situation, that the British healthcare system has a different kind of dynamism and a certain advancedness from that of the United States, and the significance of placing British medicine as one of the opposite viewpoints from which to grasp Japanese medicine in relative terms. This precious and hard-to-come-by study abroad experience was made possible only through the great efforts and warm support of the professors and administrative staff of the International Exchange Office. I would like to take this opportunity to deeply thank Professor 坂本 and Associate Professor 粕谷 of the International Exchange Office, the secretaries Ms. 山崎 and Ms. 平光, and Ms. 西尾 and Ms. 藤本 of Academic Affairs.
